chunks.text:
The difference between an angel and a VC is that angels are amateurs and VCs are pros. VCs invest other people’s money and angels invest their own on their own terms. Although some angels are quite rigorous and act very much like the pros, for the most part they are much more like hobbyists. Their decision making process is usually much faster--they can make the call all on their own--and there is almost always a much larger component of emotion that goes into that decision.  
VCs will usually require more time, more meetings, and will have multiple partners involved in the final decision. And remember, VCs see LOTS of deals and invest in very few, so you will have to stand out from a crowd.

In 2005, when Y Combinator started, there was already a well developed ecosystem of venture capital firms in Silicon Valley and Boston. But access to those venture capital firms was limited.  
VCs preferred to fund companies that already seemed like a sure bet - in other words, were far along. They also preferred to fund MBAs with previous executive experience and shied away from unproven teams with technical founders. Because they had a lock on the funding market, they asked for onerous financial terms and often replaced founders with favored executives. The only model of institutional seed funding was the “business incubator” model, where VC firms would fund well-connected founders they knew and incubate them in their office.

# Comparing Angel Funding vs. Venture Capital Dynamics

Based on the essay corpus, here are the key differences in how these funding sources operate:

## Decision-Making Speed & Process

**Angel Investors** operate with significantly faster decision cycles. According to *A Guide to Seed Fundraising*, "Their decision making process is usually much faster--they can make the call all on their own." This is because angels invest their own money on their own terms.

In contrast, **VCs require substantially more time and complexity**: "VCs will usually require more time, more meetings, and will have multiple partners involved in the final decision."

## Investment Philosophy & Selectivity

The sources reveal a fundamental difference in how each evaluates deals:

- **Angels**: Described as "amateurs" and "hobbyists" with "a much larger component of emotion that goes into that decision"
- **VCs**: Characterized as "pros" who "see LOTS of deals and invest in very few, so you will have to stand out from a crowd"

## Historical Funding Gatekeeping

*How Biotech Startup Funding Will Change in the Next 10 Years* illustrates how VCs historically held a "lock on the funding market," preferring companies "already far along" and favoring MBAs with executive experience while "shy[ing] away from unproven teams with technical founders." They demanded "onerous financial terms" and often replaced founders entirely.

This gatekeeping created space for angel investors to fill the early-stage gap that VCs were unwilling to serve.
